utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation that you made to tell the truth still applies. Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Eliott Behar. I'm counsel for the Prosecution, and I have a number of questions for you this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness's microphones were off, the interpreters did not hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, just before we get into more detailed questions, I want to make sure that I'm understanding the extent of your evidence. Both from Wednesday and from when you testified in the Milutinovic trial, and we will have a chance to go through things in more detail. Right now I would just like to see briefly if I understand your position. You are saying, sir, first of all, there were no roadblocks or check-points, certainly no barbed wire in Pristina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, what I said for the most part was what you said just now, or rather, I said that there was no barbed wire around Pristina or any check-points that prevented the unhindered movement of the population towards Pristina, outside Pristina, and within the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That's right, sir. I think, in fact, you were quite clear in your testimony there were no check-points, no barbed wire. And you were also clear there was no destruction of any Albanian religious institution, correct? Certainly no destruction of mosques; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct. Not a single Islamic place of worship in the territory of Pristina had been destroyed or damaged throughout the aggression, or rather, up until the moment when the Kumanovo agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You were also clear, sir, there were no deportations conducted by any of the Serb forces, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I did not see any such deportations and also I did not observe myself that anyone was deporting someone else by force. I'm not aware of any such thing, and I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You were also clear, sir, and you spoke in some detail about this, the Prosecution witness Nazalie Bala couldn't possibly have made any of the observations she made, just to be clear cover those, you said she certainly couldn't have seen Dragodan from where she was, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that she could not see the Orthodox cemetery in Pristina near Dragodan. As for parts of the Dragodan neighbourhood, perhaps it is possible to see them, some of them, but not the Orthodox cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: We can go through that in more detail, sir, but before we move on, you were also clear that she couldn't have seen from Vranjevac towards Kojlovica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kojlovica, yes, towards Kojlovica, I mean, but she could not see the village of Kojlovica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And you said the same thing about Lukare, she couldn't have seen it, and you also added there were no tanks or armoured vehicles there in any case, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a military depot in Lukare of the Pristina Corps, and in that part of the area, she could not see anything. She could only hear detonations from there because part of Lukare was bombed every day during the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And, in fact, sir, despite the evidence that we've heard in this case from a number of different witnesses about the events that took place in Pristina after the outbreak of the war and what took place at the hands of the Serb forces, your testimony is that things in Pristina essentially were fine, life went on as normal; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Everything was not fine in Pristina. I said that life went on in a relatively normal way in keeping with war-time conditions though. Supplies were as normal as possible. I mean, there were sufficient quantities of bread, and it was roughly as it was before the war, the bread situation. I said that cultural life functioned more or less as normal. There was TV and radio in the Siptar language, in the Serbian language, in the Turkish language, and in the Roma language. I also said that other things were going on as well in Pristina, things that are part of normal life. The market, then the hospital. Irrespective of war, children were born, people died, got married. Before the aggression, during the aggression practically there was no difference. Babies were born at the maternity ward of the Pristina hospital, and the staff there was of Siptar, Serb, Turkish ethnicity, and I know all of their names, and all of the population in Pristina was aware of that. Then in Pristina there were religious services in practically all mosques, even during the NATO aggression. Even in the three mosques that were in the immediate vicinity of my command post. That would be it in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think we have your position on that. Sir, it would appear on the whole of your testimony that in short you are denying that any of the allegations that have been made against the Serb forces who were operating in Pristina were true, and that would involve deportations, certainly murders, the use of armoured vehicles, tanks? Essential sir, none of the allegations that have been made against the Serb forces in this case are accurate in your testimony; is that a fair characterisation?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with what you said just now. It is correct that there were killings in Pristina, and it is true that there were dead among the Serbs and Siptars and other ethnicities, but for the most part, they were victims of the NATO bombing, and also of the Siptar terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But not by the Serb forces, sir, which is what I asked you? The Serb forces --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any civilian victims at the hands of the Serb forces. I'm particularly not aware of anyone being harmed from the -- or rather by the command group or the personnel that I commanded. As you know, I have already said that we had not fired a single bullet. We did not point any barrels of our weapons at anyone all the way up until the end of the NATO aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I'd like to go through your evidence on each of these points in more detail. To begin, sir, you testified in the Milutinovic case and again here that you saw columns of Kosovo Albanians fleeing Pristina, moving en masse through the city, and your testimony was that these people in the columns were pretending that they were faking. As you put it, sir, this was a "imitation of migration." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall saying that, I recall that very well. And that is, indeed, what I had seen. I actually saw this imitation several times. I can give you the details as well, what I said then and new ones that I've remembered in the meantime. Several times they passed right by my command post where I was. I even talked to certain individuals from these columns. These were fellow citizens of mine with whom I'd lived for many years, I knew many of them personally. I saw them passing by me and then coming back from another direction. I can even give you the exact directions. And that's what happened on several occasions. A part of them really did move out of town. Whereas others were involved in this imitation, as I called it. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: We'll go step by step, sir. You are also clear, sir, that the purpose of this fake migration was essentially an elaborate ruse by the population to help terrorists flee the country. If we can, I'd like to look at your exact words in Milutinovic in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could see D712, please. That's at page 44. So if we can look at line 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: The transcript is in English, sir, so I'll read it to you and you'll receive the translation. You said: "The aim" in other words the aim or the point of having these columns. "The aim, especially in the area from Ljubce to Grastica was to have terrorists join those columns who threw away their weapons and fled before the forces fighting them and shooting at them." Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall having said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to suggest to you that there are a number of problems with this claim, and I'd like to go through a number of the issues as I see them, one by one. To start with, this reason you've given, you've essentially said that the reason for this enormous production is false convoys that are moving through the city was so that the Albanians could help terrorists to flee the country. But, in fact, sir, according to your evidence, terrorists acts were continuing and, in fact, even intensifying. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that as a whole. That was just one of the reasons. One of the important reasons was to create a picture of a humanitarian catastrophe and migration. As for these columns especially when they were coming from Grastica and Kacikol, they wanted the terrorists to join these columns, or rather, the terrorists would throw away their weapons and then they would join these columns. That was a very important reason too, and it was established several times, even before the aggression but also during the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But, sir, to focus on my question, do you recall in your previous testimony discussing in some detail that terrorist attacks were continuing and even intensifying throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very intensive terrorist attacks, both during the aggression and before the aggression. It went on all the time in the broader area of Pristina, and there were many acts of terrorism committed in Pristina itself by the Siptar terrorists at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So even just on your own evidence, sir, the terrorists weren't fleeing the country at all, their operations were continuing, and yet you've described these convoys to operate for the purpose of moving terrorists out of the country? That doesn't fit together, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what I said to you. You keep saying that I've said that, but that's not what I said. It was not to have the terrorists leave the country. It was to have the terrorists become part of those columns so that they could infiltrate town again and that territory again so that they could continue carrying out their terrorist activities. So it wasn't the terrorists' aim to move out of Kosovo and Metohija, rather it was their aim to hide in the areas where they had been operating until then to become part of the columns, leave out of town, operate out of town, and then operate yet again with weapons both inside town and outside town. That is the point of what I've been trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay, sir, well, then let's take that position and let's explore it a little bit. If you had actually seen these large convoys that you knew to be smuggling terrorists on mass from one location to another, surely, sir, that's something that you would have had to duty to support to your superiors, correct? You would have had an obligation to report that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only that it would have been my duty, I did that anyway. Even if I had not done that, my Superior Command knew about this from the previous period before the aggression too. That was the method applied by the Siptar terrorists. Similar methods were applied by them earlier on, too, like in 1990 when they pretended to fall dead because they had been allegedly poisoned by the Serbian forces. An entire class of school children would fall in the middle of the classroom, Siptar school children; whereas, Serb school children would just look at them and wonder what on earth was going on, so the methodology is very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Let's try to stay focused on the questions here, sir. You've agree, I think, that you would have had an obligation certainly to report on this massive terrorist activity, so I ask you, sir, where are those reports?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many reports of mine that are devoted to that. I reported to the corps commander about that orally as well. I also reported to the corps command during the aggression. I also remember that I filed written reports several times, and I really do wonder where these reports may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you, sir, we certainly haven't seen a single one of those reports here. Before we move on --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't find these reports either. I tried to find some of them, but I couldn't because my access to archives became impossible because of the lack of care for these archives in Belgrade. And because of the attitude of the authorities that organise these archives and treat them in a certain way. To this day, I cannot get a single document that I signed during the aggression. For example, I signed a document allowing the establishment of a bathroom in Grmija so that all members of the military could take baths. I also signed a document stating how mail should be received at the Pristina garrison. That document isn't there either, and there are eye-witnesses to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, sir, there may certainly be differences in obtaining documents relating to the establishment of a bathroom as compared to documents establishing a massive large-scale operation to move terrorists throughout Pristina, but let me move on. Another point, sir, and I'll put this to you directly, it seems problematic --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: On the one hand, sir, you are saying that these were fake convoys that were moving back and forth throughout Pristina, but you've also said repeatedly in your testimony that the Kosovo Albanians did, in fact, leave Pristina but they only left in order to escape the NATO bombing. We can go through this step by step, sir. Let me ask you first, do you recall testifying that the Kosovo Albanians left Pristina because of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is quite certain that they were leaving just like the Serbs. Siptars were leaving Pristina and the broader region because of the NATO aggression, but Serbs were leaving it too. Also, I indicated this other very important reason. This imitation, this false representation of immigration. So there were examples of both. And then there were also examples of a third and fourth kind of emigration, but I also said that there were examples of immigration into Pristina, that is to say, Siptars and Serbs moving into Pristina. There are many diverse reasons and types of emigration and immigration. However, the most massive movements of both Serbs and Siptars were due to NATO bombings and many casualties among the Siptars and Serbs due to these attacks and everything that happened due to panic and propaganda in the town of Pristina. Especially attacks against infrastructure, waterworks, the telephone exchange in Pristina, the transformer station, there were power cuts every day, and especially the human casualties that were suffered, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, if you can, let's try to keep your answers focused and you'll have a chance to expand on the aspects of your answers that focus on my question. Just very briefly, sir, you've said that these large movements out of Pristina began on the eve of the aggression and continued and, in fact, intensified through the aggression. Very briefly, sir, is that fair, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly put, there was immigration out of Pristina and the general area of Pristina before the aggression, during the aggression, as well as after the aggression. The same goes for people moving in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And, sir, perhaps we'll just deal with this by looking at your brief testimony in the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we can see D712 again at page 43. Beginning at line 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You were quite focused here, sir, in discussing the population moving out of Pristina and you say: "It grew in intensity," as in the migration, "grew in intensity especially after the air-strikes of the very centre of town, which was on the 7th of April. After that, this migration increased, especially because some crucial facilities, such as the transformer station in Pristina were bombed." You essential repeated that on Wednesday, sir. Do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that was recorded then and everything I said then is something I cannot deny now, and I don't want to. I recall this. I know that people were moving out of Pristina in greater numbers after the 7th of April including Albanian, Serbs and others because there were many victims. There were many Serbs and Siptars killed during the bombing. Telephone lines were interrupted and people were in panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So, sir, your position is that somehow you were you able to tell that some of the Albanians were putting on a fake show and pretending to leave in large convoys while others were actually leaving in convoys, but those others were only leaving because of the NATO bombing. Does that make sense, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a synchronised process. Some of them were imitating the existence of a column by going around Pristina in circles. Others moved out because of the fear of NATO bombardment and the casualties they had suffered trying to bring their children to safety. There were also cases of people moving out of Pristina for fear of the Siptar terrorists activities, as well as losses they had experienced in particular because of their activities. But there were also great numbers of Siptars moving into Pristina because the terrorists were particularly active in the general area of Pristina, especially in the area of Drenica and Malisevo. They were moving into Pristina seeking refuge. Some of that Albanian population was received by the Red Cross in Pristina as well as by other local authority organs in charge of that. People were received and given assistance. Some of them were even received in the area of Kisnica, only 1- to 200 metres away from the corps command building. Those Siptars had come from Drenica and Malisevo. They were received there together with the Serbs in the refugee centre. They were given the same assistance they -- that was accorded to the Serbs who had previously arrived from Croatia and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, please try, if you can, to focus on my questions and what you are actually being asked. Sir, you've described what is no doubt an extremely complicated state of affairs that it appears you were able to discern from watching, perhaps even from just watching out your window. But, sir, I'm going to suggest to you that what, in fact, took place and the explanation for what you are saying was, in fact, much simpler. My suggestion to you, sir, is that you essentially adopted the position that was taken in the Milutinovic Defence, which was that the Albanians left because of the NATO bombing, and that you've added, as well, your own explanation, which is that the Albanians didn't leave at all, they essential just walked back and forth in the same convoys but that you found now, sir, that those positions don't fit together so you've come up with what is a rather complicated and hard-to-fathom state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have said quite a lot here. I'm trying to analyse that because you put a number of questions as well as a number of assertions. I'll try to be concise. I agree with you that the situation was complex and that the reasons for people of moving in or moving out were as complex, including those who tried to imitate a process of moving out. What is the gist of it all? Part of the Serb and Albanian population had moved prior to the aggression as well as during the aggression. Parts of the population moved out because of the fear of NATO bombardment. I have explained that in length. There were many casualties, entire Albanian families were killed by NATO bombs as well as many Serbs in Pristina. Next some of them were moving out because they feared the Siptar terrorists. Thirdly, a number of families of Siptar terrorists as well as those related to them from the general area of Pristina moved out because they feared retaliation since their family members were members of the terrorist forces. Fourthly, some people were moving out because the situation in town was difficult. There were power cuts, there were no telephone lines, and they could not speak to their nearest and dearest. There were many other reasons for people moving out as well as moving in, as I've said. When we are talking about emigration, one should always bear in mind that Serbs, Roma, Albanians, the Turks, and everyone else was moving out in different ways, on foot, in vehicle, on buses, and I've already explained my role in --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You've covered that already. Sir, if I can just get back again to the core of my question, which is the inconsistency between these two basic claims, in fact, the inconsistency was first pointed out to you by His Honour Judge Bonomy when you testified in the Milutinovic case, and perhaps we can look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: It's at again D712. It's at page -- I only have the transcript reference for this, it's T-19194. If we can have that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we just look here at line 18, sir, I think we'll see that your explanation here is relatively more straightforward, and it appears to have become more and more complex. At line 18 Judge Bonomy asks you: "Are these different columns from the ones that were migrating to escape the bombs?" And he appears to be have been somewhat surprised by your position there, and you responded: "Well, my answer is as follows: Some of those columns behaved in the way I have just described. Some citizens really fled to escape the bombs. They were concerned and frightened of the bombing. Some had had relatives killed or wounded by the bombs. And these were civilians fleeing." Then you said: "However, there were many of those that I've just described who were simply pretending to migrate, and these were more numerous than the former category. At least as far as the town of Pristina is concerned." Do you recall that exchange with Judge Bonomy, sir, that answer?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully recall this answer. I see nothing that would be in dispute in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And so your answer when you were first met with this inconsistency was a simple one, there were different columns of Albanians moving throughout the city, some of those you were able to tell were fake convoys but others were real convoys, and you were apparently also able to tell that those people were only leaving because of the NATO bombing. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I said is correct for sure. There's no reason for it to be any other way other than the way I described it and the way I experienced it. I can confirm the same thing now. I used to see citizens in columns who would move about Pristina in the morning and then in the afternoon they would pass by me again. I recognised among them Adem Demaci as one of those escorting those columns, he was a famous terrorist. He was always part of that column and always came back. He didn't leave Pristina for a single day. He moved about safely. He did not flee; whereas, I saw many others who did pass by and never returned. That's the essence. I see nothing in dispute or anything contradictory in my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think we have your position on that point, sir. Let's move to a slightly different topic. Sir, you came here on Wednesday and on your own you went into detail about depleted uranium. And if we can, let's look at one of those passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could look at the testimony from Wednesday from this case, that's T-11559. I'm told that we can actually bring that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we just look at beginning at line 19, you were asked, the question was a simple one: "Did you have any information about -- about what was used in the bombing? What kind of equipment?" Your answer was: "I had a lot of information. I had practically daily insight." And then you went on to say, "I can document many things from that field, particularly the fact that the broader area of Pristina was bombed with projectiles that contained depleted uranium." Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you had, in fact, never mentioned anything before about depleted uranium, had you, in this court, when you testified in the Milutinovic trial, you never used the words "depleted uranium," had you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall everything I said, but it must be recorded. What is on the record is something I must have said. And let me tell you this: I haven't uttered many a thing and I won't even today because there is simply no time. I could go on and on about the methods and means used against the population of Kosovo, Serbs, Albanian, Turks, Roma and others. The plight was so great that it is difficult for me to go through all of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I know you can't sir, and let's just focus on my question. I think tell you that you, in fact, never mentioned the words "depleted uranium." You certainly never mentioned it in the Milutinovic case, but you did, in fact, discuss the NATO bombing at great length during your testimony. Would you agree with that, sir, you did, in fact, go into great detail about the NATO bombing, correct? Just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke extensively about NATO bombardment. In the last case, the Milutinovic case, I didn't mention any planes that were shot down, but that could have been seen by many inhabitants of Pristina. There are many things I didn't mention but nonetheless, they took place in Pristina and its broader area. I didn't even mention many chemical incidents, although such things occurred, many inhabitants of Pristina suffered from such attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And yet, sir, despite not having mentioned this when you testified in detail about people fleeing the city because of NATO bombing, you are now saying that you had firsthand knowledge of depleted uranium use and, in fact, sir, you've testified that you were personally handling and dealing with depleted uranium projectiles out in the field, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Did you discuss this issue about depleted uranium with anyone before you testified here today, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I discussed that topic a few years ago constantly with other citizens, friends of mine from the army and outside the army about depleted uranium. There were many entities that undertook checks about the effects of such ammunition. There were many of them handling that issue before and now there are less and less because unfortunately it seems to be the policy now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Just to focus again on the very specific question, sir. Before you testified here on Wednesday, before you began your testimony, did you discuss the issue of depleted uranium with anyone, I can be specific, did you discuss it with anyone who had an interest in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that. I did not discuss it that way, and there was no need for me. I was not trying to gain additional information. I'm only talking about what I could see and observe myself. Many people suffered the consequences of such attacks, and many people are still being treated for consequences of that type of ammunition including the military, medical clinic, and other health institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that issues surrounding depleted uranium seem to now have become an issue in this case? Is that something that you are aware of or that you were aware of before you began your testimony on Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before my arrival here, I heard that depleted uranium was discussed here among other things. It was used, it is a generally known thing, and I don't think that needs to be proven separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, how did you hear that depleted uranium was being discussed here?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of depleted uranium being discussed here in the Milutinovic case. As far as I recall, it was a topic then as well. As well as later. I could read in our press about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, we've already covered the fact that you didn't mention depleted uranium once when you testified in the Milutinovic case. What I'd like to know is that you mentioned "before my arrival here, I heard that depleted uranium was discussed here among other things." What I would like to know is, how did you hear that, who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, from the media. I heard of the use off uranium from the media. I also had that information during the aggression because our units tasked with providing anti-nuclear and chemical security measures were familiar with that. I knew about that at the time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I know that, sir, what I'm trying to focus on is how you discovered that it was an issue in this case before you testified. You are saying that you heard that in the media. Do you mean, sir, that you read in the media that the use of depleted uranium was being used in the Djordjevic case? Am I understanding that correctly? This was being discussed, this was now an issue?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go much into it the Djordjevic case. I was here for other tasks and duties as well. I'm not particularly interested in this case. I could follow the media just as any other citizen. As for the use of depleted uranium in Kosovo, I received information from the media. I think it was carried by the world press as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, sir, it doesn't seem like I'm going to get an answer from you with respect to where you heard this information or if you spoke to anyone before coming here on Wednesday, but I'll put to you, sir, the suggestion that, in fact, what has happened here is that you've received information somehow that depleted uranium, the use of depleted uranium, is a live issue in this case, and you've therefore come and testified in detail about your personal experience with depleted uranium on the ground in Kosovo in order to further that line of defence. Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. There's no reason to back anyone up in particular or further anything. I told you that I had information of such missiles myself. There are many witnesses to that, I even organised an exhibition in front of my command building to the north-west of the Pristina mosque. All citizens could see that there were Tomahawk stabilisers, cluster bombs stabilisers, and parts of cluster bombs. There were signatures of personnel who put their signatures on parts of those ammunitions. The TV Belgrade took footage of that. Magoci [phoen] was the cameraman, and the reporter was another Albanian. The whole world could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, while we were on the topic of depleted uranium, let me take you to particular portion of your testimony on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could see again from the Djordjevic trial, T-11560. And we'll look beginning at line 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You were asked, sir, of the question: "I asked you about the location where you were where depleted uranium was used and how come you know?" And you answered: "I caught these projectiles with my own hands in the area of Donja Grmija. That is the untoward thing that I did. And I brought them to Pristina so that all citizens could see them. And, to this day, I suffer the effects of that." Now, unless you are a truly remarkable man, sir, I'm assuming that you didn't actually catch a projectile with your hands, perhaps that was an error of interpretation, but if I understand what you are saying correctly, you are testifying that you picked up a depleted uranium projectile with your own hands; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not. I don't know what you gathered from that, but I would very much like you to understand what I'm trying to say. I took parts of those projectiles, there's nothing in question there. There are countless witnesses to that. There seems to be a mistake, though, and I stand to be corrected if I'm wrong, I don't think it was in the area of Grmija. Even if it was, there is no problem there. I think it was Brnjica, although in the general area of Grmija there were parts of such missiles found. So the general area of Pristina, Gornja Brnjica , Donija Brnjica, the general area of Devet Jugovica, and other parts of on the outskirts of Pristina. We collected such missile parts. I even wanted to present you with a list of those parts. We put up an entire exhibition in front of the building command, both Siptars and Serbs could see it. At the time it served as an encouragement to the citizens in order to convince them not to move out. We were trying to tell them, well, if we are holding these pieces in our hands, then they are not a danger to you, but it seems that we were wrong believing they wouldn't leave no matter what.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, sir, your testimony is that you picked up a projectile or at least parts of a projectile that had fallen from a plane and presumably not exploded, and you not only carried it around yourself but you brought it back to show to civilians; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My primary intention was not to show it to the civilians. We put them there in front of the building so that we could see them and whoever would pass by, Serb, Siptars, whoever would pass by. Let the population see them, that's why we brought them there. You say unexploded, I don't know how come you said that because I never said that. I guess that I have enough military training to know not to take any unexploded projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's a simple question, sir, but if it had exploded, then would you have anything to bring back?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, of course I would. Do you know of the theory that there is no perpetuum mobile so you can find scattered about pieces on the ground. Even when aircraft exploded, there were parts scattered about in a wide area. To this day, there are some parts of that aircraft at the museum in Surcin near Belgrade. There's always something left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, just before we move on, there's something I'm having trouble understanding. You just testified that your primary intention was not to show it, these projectiles, to civilians, but if we look up to line 15 of page 21, you in fact, said something to the effect that at the time you put these, used these projectiles as an encouragement to the citizens. I see I've lost the reference on the page, but it appears, sir, that you just testified that you put these pieces of projectiles in front of your building in order to show to civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Viewed from this distance, that's exactly the way it seemed. If we are standing by them, then there's no reason for civilians to run away from them. Let them see what was thrown on all of us, irrespective of ethnicity. That was done from submarines in the Mediterranean, from the Adriatic Sea, from the air. Let them see what was being thrown at all of us together, so now what is in dispute there? The fact that they saw it? That we all saw it? That there is television footage showing that? TV Belgrade recorded that, and then it was broadcast by media all over the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think your position is clear, sir, and what you've said is that, just to back this up, sir, you've spent your career in the military, you certainly understand and know projectiles well, and you know what would be dangerous and what would not, and you took these projectiles and you, in fact, put on a display to show the civilians of Pristina that there was nothing to fear here. Is that fair to say, sir, I think I just repeated your evidence back to you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, no, I said what I said, and now the way you recounted it doesn't really turn out exactly the way I had put it, but the point is that it wasn't only me. My associates as well were involved in this. I didn't go to pick all of this up by myself. It's not that I just happened to know that these projectiles were found somewhere. I was -- I received information that there were pieces in various parts and then I went there with my officers and NCOs and also the British KFOR troops saw that because they came there, they took up the area around the mosque. When I left, as I was leaving, I saw them see the projectiles too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So sir, what you've said, again just to sum this up and put it back to you, you, sir, as a man who spent a career in the military, picked up and handled parts of a projectile that you say contained depleted uranium, you then brought that back, and you bought on a display to show to the civilians that there was nothing to be feared here. So surely then, sir, civilians, Albanian civilians, would not be fleeing because of depleted uranium fragments that had been dropped on Kosovo. Do you agree with that? Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I do not agree with you that that is the way you can put it. There were areas because they were marked or rather, our units had the duty to mark certain areas especially units that were in charge of PN HBO, that is to say, anti-nuclear chemical warfare focused on the 52nd Battalion, the ABHO Battalion that was commanded by then Captain 1st Class Aleksic Andric. Areas were marked, then the possibility was indicated, or rather, before the aggression there was certain knowledge of that possibility, I'm not sure now, but I think that the media also reported about that possibility. Not only in our country in Serbia or rather, in Yugoslavia but also worldwide, the projectiles with the depleted uranium could be used, and after all 30.000, over 30.000 projectiles were used in Kosovo and Metohija or rather, our country that was established later on. That is the figure as far as depleted uranium is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Let's not engage in a wild speculation here, sir. What I'm saying very simply is, at first, you a trained military man, someone who knows projectiles well and is surrounded by people with expertise, you even talk about chemical units, you are saying you went and picked up fragments that contained depleted uranium, so obviously you are not fearful and had apparently no reason to be fearful at that time given what you knew, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would not agree with all of that that you said because I mean, well, I'm not much of an expert for that. I'm an expert in a great many other things in the military, but I knew that in addition to other things. I expressed an interest, and after all, I passed a test in that area. I even took tests in the field of the air force in general in the navy, et cetera, so this is an auxiliary thing as far as I'm concerned, but there's no doubt that I know a great deal. Irrespective of that knowledge, I did what I did, and it wasn't my first time. I knew that explosives were dangerous, but once in 1972 I had a small accident in respect of that and after all, many people do things against their actual knowledge and then they suffer the consequences. And I don't see anything that is questionable in all of this that I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Let's of move briefly now, if we can, to a different topic. You testified, sir, about some leaflets that were found in Pristina that had asked the Albanians to leave the country. Do you recall testifying to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could see P419. Also actually if we could see it in the original Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, is this the leaflet you were referring to? It appears to be the same in content as the exhibit you referred to in Milutinovic, but perhaps you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the leaflet. That's it. You can see the red colour now as opposed to earlier on, so yes, that is the leaflet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And, I just want to be clear, sir, before we move on, on Wednesday when us testified you mentioned that NATO had dropped leaflets from a plane, but that wasn't this KLA leaflet which -- that you discussed in your Milutinovic testimony, was it? Let me restate the question. It wasn't this KLA leaflet that was dropped from a NATO plane, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably it wasn't. I cannot confirm whether that was or was not the case, but most probably that was not the case because when these leaflets were found, at that time I have no information to the effect that they were seen in the air or found in the air. They were found on the ground, as opposed to the leaflets or flyers that were dropped from planes because you could see them falling after NATO aircraft would fly by especially B-52s.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And perhaps if we could see, this is again from the Djordjevic trial, T-11378.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: This is the testimony of Milos Dosan. Sir, you may be familiar with him. He states, this is at line 22, looking at the same leaflet: "Yes, I'm familiar with this leaflet, but it was not dropped from aircraft." Again he reiterates that a couple of times. Is that consistent with your understanding as well?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know General Milos Dosan, he is a good friend of mine from the days of the aggression and later on as well. As for this particular statement, I would like to ask you to repeat it to me so that I could give you a more precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. I'm really just showing you Mr. Dosan's testimony. He had indicated on several occasions that he was familiar with this leaflet but that it was not dropped from an aircraft. Actually, if we can scroll down to 11379, line 19. He says there: "These leaflets were found across town, they were not dropped from aircraft, and an officer brought them to the command." Again, is that consistent, sir, with your experience? These were not leaflets that were dropped from aircraft and were, in fact, found throughout town?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My experience should be similar to that, or rather, I assume that it had not been dropped from aircraft because the persons who brought this leaflet to me, and I have already said that I had found a leaflet like that by myself in Pristina, so the persons who found this one told me that they found it on the ground. I never looked up and I did not see it falling from an aircraft. So it is my assumption, therefore, that it had not been dropped from an aircraft, and I think that the assumption is well-founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Now, it was, in fact, a practice that the MUP sometimes used to distribute leaflets to the population, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of that practice. I didn't observe it, at any rate. If you have some information, well, I cannot go into that. I do not remember that because that was not within my job description to register that and remember that. Even if that did happen, I personally do not remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: For example, sir, in late 1998, the MUP used leaflets asking certain Kosovo Albanians to return to their villages. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that, but my memory is hazy. As for the concentration of my thoughts, I did not focus on that. My preoccupations were different, within my own line of work, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can we see P483, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Perhaps this may be familiar to you, sir. If we just look at page 2 at the bottom, it's the first bullet point under the third section there. It says -- this is actually diplomatic correspondence from the Austrian embassy, sir, but they're addressing the point that we just discussed that you recall but you said your memory is a bit hazy. It's a comment that they say: "Text of MUP flyer and way of distribution not the right way to encourage the return of IDPs." And what that's referring to is the MUP's use of flyers, as we've discussed, to communicate with the Albanian populace. Perhaps that may not refresh your memory too much, but does that assist you in any way in remembering anything about this flyer, or this practice?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for this guidance. However, as regards this document, I can hardly be of any assistance to you. It's not for lack of wanting. I mean, I would really like to help you, you but objectively speaking I cannot hardly say anything to you about this document because I haven't got a lot of information about it or rather, I have no information. I told you that I was involved in a different line of work. Irrespective of that, I have no recollection of this. I am available to you to answer all your questions that have to do with things that I do know, but I don't think that I can be of much use in this particular regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think you've told us what you recall, and I appreciate that. As someone who has extensive experience in the army, sir, would you agree that propaganda is a tool that's sometimes or often used in times of war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree with you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And, in fact, sir, we've had specific evidence in this case that the Serb forces distributed these leaflets, the KLA leaflet that you were looking at, as part of a propaganda campaign to have the Albanians leave Kosovo. I'll take you to a specific passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could see, this is again from the Djordjevic case, it's T-2232. So just to be clear, it's the transcript reference from Djordjevic T-2232. It's witness -- it's the testimony of Adnan Merovci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is Adem Demaqi [as interpreted], is he a well-known terrorist. He was convicted on several occasions and served over 20 years in prison in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'll give you a chance to comment on that. What I'm interested, sir, is a comment on the content of what he said, not on his general reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought that the interpreter had indicated to us that there was a mistake. We heard that that was the witness Adem Demaqi who was heard in these proceedings. I would just like to tell my colleague Mr. Behar to know that I mean, so that he could tell us exactly what the name of the witness was, because obviously it wasn't heard properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I appreciate that, for my learned friend. It was Adnan Merovci is the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, this is the testimony of Mr. Merovci. You may know him, he lived in Pristina, and he worked closely with Mr. Rugova. I'd like to have your comment on this passage, just on the content of what he is saying. If we look at line 20, he's asked: "Did you have the opportunity to see any of these pamphlets that were distributed?" And he answers that he saw them in the hallway before the entrance to his flat. And he goes on to say: "I took it -- took a copy of it and saw that it was mere propaganda, both in terms of its content and the way it was formulated, general layout of the pamphlet. It contained many errors, and there was a discrepancy between what it said and the insignia and the person who had signed it. On top, there was a KLA insignia and then signed below it was signed by Mr. Rugova. When, as you well know, Mr. Rugova led the LDK and the Kosovo liberation army was led by other people. This shows that it was a way to strike fear and panic among the population, because that, the text was full of mistakes in Albanian which shows it was not done by professionals." And he goes on somewhat in that vein but he is asked just below: "And at the time did Mr. Rugova have any sort of contact with the KLA?" And he responds: "No, he did not." Now, sir, I wanted to invite your comment on Mr. Merovci's testimony in that regard. First, that this was a document of propaganda. Second, that there's a discrepancy between the KLA heading and a signature by Mr. Rugova when, in fact, Mr. Rugova was not even in contact with the KLA at that time. Can you comment on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since you are putting this question to me, I shall try to be of assistance to you and to give you some comments. First of all, this mistake that happened, the name I heard in interpretation was Adem Demaqi, later on it was correct, so it's Adnan Merovci, no problem whatsoever. As for that flyer or leaflet, I cannot deal with it in depth in terms of which way this analysis is going, whether it is this or that type of propaganda. At any rate, it is propaganda. Now, what kind of mistakes are involved and whether there are any, I cannot really help you very much on that either. However, as to whether it is contrary to the ideas of the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army, in fact, these are terrorists forces and somebody called named them the liberation army or named them the liberation army because that's what suited their purposes, and Mr. Rugova, well, I really could not speak about that. That is a generally known thing, that there were different lines involved, a soft line and a hard-line, part of the movement, but all of these wings and fractions were aimed in the same direction, and that direction is terrorist activity, and the main objective was the cessation of Kosovo and Metohija from Serbia contrary to international law and contrary to the constitution, laws, et cetera. So these were wings that had some views that differed but their objective was the same. By way of assistance to you, that would be my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I know that you don't know who produced the leaflet, but does it not seem clear to you that material like this would have been produced by the Serb forces, because it was the Serb forces, if anyone, who wanted the Albanians to leave the territory, not the Albanians. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with that. I completely disagree because, first of all, this was never produced by the Serb forces, nor would have the Serb forces ever produced that kind of thing. Especially not for the purpose of moving the Siptars out of Kosovo and Metohija. The Serb forces produced many things in order to have a larger population in Kosovo and Metohija, not to have the population move out. The authorities of Serbia built infrastructure in Kosovo and Metohija, promoted health care, education, population levels. As a matter of fact, they did their best to have the Serbian population move out and the Siptar population remain there. That is tellingly demonstrated by statistics and a whole lot of other things and after all, you have all that information available to you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you have already been clear that your position is that the KLA wanted Kosovo to be an independent state for the Kosovo Albanians. You just, in fact, said a couple of minutes ago that the main objective was the cessation of Kosovo from Serbia. Given that state of affairs, sir, why on earth would the KLA or anyone else on the Albanian side be trying to get the Albanians to flee the country and leave it to the Serbs? Does that make any sense?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It makes all the sense there is. You also put a question a minute ago to that effect. Of course it makes sense. When you were putting a question, you said that many in the world use propaganda, and I confirmed it to be true. If it were not, Hitler would not have burned down Reichstag and accused someone else for it. I guess you are familiar with that. It's basic literature. That's what propaganda is for, to accuse someone else for one's own benefit. And to twist the reality. Such propaganda was used by the NATO Alliance as well, because they were delivering pamphlets from the B-52 airplanes. Many lies were contained there, for example, the name of Zeljko Pekovic, a major, is stated as the commander of the 52nd Military Police Battalion. Whereas it is obvious that this leaflet was drafted in NATO before the aggression because that major in question handed over that battalion in June 1998 to Major Zeljko Kopanja. He was the newer commander, whereas the old commander went to attend the staff school and yet we had this leaflet with his name dropped from a plane. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think I'm losing track of you a little bit, I think we may have gone a little far off base. What I'm trying to understand, sir, is how it would make any sense if the intention of the KLA was to create an independent Kosovo, a state essentially as you are saying, for Albanians and how did does it make sense for the KLA to be asking or demanding that all the Albanians leave Kosovo? Those two things seem antithetical to me.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think these are two contradictory things. They are in close relation in order to put up an appearance of a humanitarian catastrophe so that the NATO Alliance can have justification for their actions. And I believe you also know how close the co-operation was between the NATO Alliance and Siptar terrorist forces. You saw the photographs in which Clark and Jackson and Tachi are shaking hands and kissing. It's a generally known thing, those pictures toured the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, these leaflets were distributed -- I know I'm running slightly over, maybe I'll just try and wrap up this area. These leaflets were distributed at the outset of the bombing, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. Whose leaflets were found all across the territory of Pristina and the general area of it? That's what I know. Later on I heard that they could be found elsewhere as well. However, I'm only talking about Pristina and its general area, in the areas which were bombed and in others which were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: But the leaflets that you were talking about, sir, that you found or that were given to you, those were distributed after the bombing, as I understand it, correct? I'm not sure we picked up the interpretation, but your answer was yes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Many leaflets were found. However, these leaflets, this red one signed by Rugova and the so-called KLA or the Siptar terrorist organisation, such pamphlets were found in Pristina. I've already told you that I found one and brought it in. There were other leaflets that were found thrown out of airplanes with the picture of the flying fortress B-52. All unit commanders were called to surrender otherwise they would be flattened by carpet bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I think we are going off topic here.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And after such a threat --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I do want to follow that up, but I see we are already over our time for the break. Perhaps this is a good time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have our first break. We will resume at five minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, just before we begin again, I'm going to ask if you can really make an effort to focus on my questions and answer as briefly as possible. I will give you a chance, as we go forward, to answer other specific areas, but we do only have a limited amount of time. When we left off before the break, sir, you had said that the KLA may have distributed these leaflets or that they may have been distributed, I suppose, by anyone to put up an appearance of a humanitarian catastrophe to justify NATO getting involved. But, in fact, sir, by the time these leaflets were distributed and certainly by the time you encountered them, the NATO bombing had already started, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be concise in my answers so that we may save some time together. I always try not to have to mention the abbreviation KLA, and even if I do, you should bear in mind that I mean the Siptar terrorist forces. It is true that they used any available means to influence the population, depending on their goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop you again, I don't want to get off on the wrong track here. My question is a very specific one. At the time that you found this leaflet, had the NATO bombing already commenced?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The period when I found that leaflet, although I don't recall the date, but it was definitely after the 24th of March, 1999, to the best of my recollection, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, when we had looked earlier at the KLA leaflet, you could see that it purports to be from Ibrahim Rugova, signed by Mr. Rugova as president of the Republic of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could see P286, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I can tell you that Mr. Rugova, in fact, testify about this issue in the Milosevic trial, he was asked about this leaflet by Mr. Milosevic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we look at page 141. At line 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic asks him: "You are appealing to the population of Kosovo to go to Albania and to Macedonia?" Mr. Rugova responds: "This is not true. This was issued in the first days of the bombing, so as you can see in the document, here is the stamp of the KLA and the signature of the president of Kosova, but it's not my document and it's clearly not of the KLA. I don't know who did it, but it was circulated in Prishtina. It was a forged document of some kind, either the police, or Belgrade, or the troops, or other people, they did it." So, sir, Mr. Rugova has been clear that he had no part in drafting this leaflet, that it was not from the KLA. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not, but judging by the words of Mr. Rugova, there is nothing in question here. He may well be right. He probably said the truth, that he was not behind it. But as far as I could see, at least from what I could hear you said, was that Mr. Rugova said "or some other people." This phrase is very important. I don't know who created it, but I can suppose. It is quite certain that it was created by the Siptar terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, we've heard already evidence that these leaflets were distributed to several parts of the city. The people who could circulate freely within Pristina at the beginning of the bombing were, in fact, the military, the police, possibly paramilitary groups and no one else. Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. Not at all. And this is why, I will be very brief. Please bear with me. Take the example of Ms. Nazalie Bala and Miomir Irovci [phoen]. These two witnesses appeared here, they freely moved about town in Pristina itself and its general area. One day after another. And one of them even left Kosovo and returned on a number of occasions completely freely, and they could speak of what they saw in the entire town, and Ms. Nazalie Bala even said that she went to work regularly crossing the Dragodan bridge on the way. This is in brief terms. One would freely move about Pristina and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, that was certainly not Ms. Bala's testimony. This Court has heard that evidence, and I will return to that topic. Let me move to a different topic. Sir, we discussed that one of your claims was that the Albanians left Kosovo, and in particular left Pristina because of the NATO bombing, we know that was part of what you said. Sir, you testified that Gracanica was very close to Pristina, correct? Was about 8 or 9 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Gracanica is quite close to Pristina. Well, we can discuss the term "relative," but I used to live there. I went to school to Gracanica. In any case, one could say it's close.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I know that you know the village well, sir, and I know that you told us as well that is where your father from, but Gracanica is essentially a Serbian village, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part in Gracanica, there has always been the Serbs in the majority. There is a number of Roma families and a single Siptar family. It is the Lekaj family, Nikola Lekaj's family. He lived there before the aggression and continued working there during and after the aggression baking bread. It is the only family there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think you were just about to say it was the -- perhaps we'll leave that, sir, but it was, in fact, the largest -- had the largest Serbian population in Kosovo, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In terms of the number of Serbs, that village had the greatest number of Serbs in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And you told us on Wednesday that you had, in fact, toured that town during the war and you were there several times, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did tour it and pass through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You were also very clear in your testimony on Wednesday that Gracanica was bombed very heavily by NATO, in fact, you said they were essentially bombed every single day by NATO; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that I had in mind the general area of Gracanica. That is correct. Many citizens of Gracanica could feel the consequences. Even the Gracanica monastery was damaged. Many walls cracked. It is an ancient monastery from 1250.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you're also very clear in your testimony that life in Gracanica went on as usual, and I can quote back to you here. You said -- this reference for my friend is at T-11539, line 16. You stated: "So life went on in Gracanica just as usual although the area around Gracanica was bombed practically every day by NATO." And you repeated again at line 20: "Detonations were heard every day but life went on unhindered as much as possible." So in fact, sir, this Serbian village was being bombed heavily by NATO every day but life went on as usual, people weren't fleeing town, they certainly weren't streaming across the borders, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is partially true. Many inhabitants of Gracanica moved out, but a lot of people remained living there. In Gracanica there was even a post office which covered the general area. In that post office throughout the aggression all citizens came to collect their pensions there. Among others, the Siptars from the village of Mramor, Slivovo, Ajvalija, Suskovac [phoen], Dragovac, so even Siptars came there on mass to collect their pensions throughout the aggression in the centre of Gracanica unhindered, and Nikola Lekaj was baking bread there, he is a Siptar from Gracanica, and he was never bothered whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think we have your answer, sir, which is that people remained living there, and we have your prior testimony that life went on as usual. But, sir, it would seem a little backward to me that NATO was fighting against Serb forces not against the Albanians certainly, one would think that if anyone would flee the NATO bombing, it would have been those Serbians -- those Serb civilians living in the Serb village that's being bombed every day, but they did not flee, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. Part of the population fled, the other part stayed. Well, they didn't flee, they simply moved away. Although, most of them remained, some left though. Secondly, Siptars as well as Serbs suffered from NATO bombardment. One needs to bear in mind, there were casualties in both groups, dead and wounded. There is statistical data and you could easily get by that although I don't think that's the goal here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I know that, sir, and I certainly don't dispute it. If we could move to another topic, sir. There were a couple of interesting slips or what appeared to me to be slips that you made when you testified in the Milutinovic case. I'd like to give you a chance to address them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could look at page 31 of your Milutinovic testimony. It's D712. Page 31. Is that page 31?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked by counsel for the Defence about the suggestion that Serbian artillery had fired from a position in Vranjevac to Kojlovica village. And you responded that the army couldn't have fired from there but you went on to say this, and this is at line 24 just after the comma. You said: "... And even if they had fired, if they could have fired, it would never have used artillery against civilians, especially since Kojlovica is a mixed village populated by both Serbs and Albanians --" At that point you were interrupted by counsel. Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall having said so. I see nothing in question there, and I certainly cannot any detect any slips. I can explain that in further detail if you are interested to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'll --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'll ask you specifically, sir, but it would appear that what you were saying in that line is that the Serb forces might have used artillery against Albanian civilians but they would certainly not fire on Serb civilians; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not. You say would or would not. I said what I said. It's in the transcript. What is true is the following: Our artillery was never there, and it never opened fire on Kojlovica. Such fire could not have been seen by Nazalie Bala because it simply didn't happen, and even if it had, she would not have been able to see it. From Lapska Street Number 30, you cannot see that. Let's move on. I also said that ultimately there is a Serb population living there as well, that's yet another possibility. Otherwise, they would never have opened fire on civilians. They never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, let's follow that up. You've been clear in your evidence that from the outbreak of the war there were no tanks or combat units in Pristina at all, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know there were none. I didn't see them, and I had no such information. There were no tanks in Pristina, and especially not -- especially not similar to what I said about Kojlovica in the locations for which it is claimed they were seen. And I insist on the word "especially" so that you wouldn't turn this against me and try to show it as a lie. There were none and especially not where people would have you believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, regardless of the use of the word "especially," sir, or any other qualifying terms you were very clear when you testified in Milutinovic that there was not a single combat unit deployed nor a single tank anywhere in Pristina. And we can just very briefly look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we can see D712, page 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You say there, sir, at line 15. You say: "As for the second, from the start of the aggression until the end, not a single combat unit was deployed there, especially not with a tank ..." And you go on to reference the 15th Armour Brigade leaving town and you go on in that sentence to say: "... From that time on there were no tanks in Pristina." And if we look at well, perhaps I won't take you to it, but at page 4 of that same transcript, sir, you again had reiterated: "There was not a single combat unit there," meaning in Pristina. "... all combat units were relocated when the aggression began from the town of Pristina." Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And you had referenced specifically the 15th Armoured Brigade and you stated that they had moved out before the aggression, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can we see P928, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You see at the top there, sir, it says "Pristina Corps Command?"

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we look at the bottom of page 1, the final paragraph under number 2, I'll just indicate the date on this document, sir, is the 1st of April, 1999. It states: "The 15th Armoured Brigade using part of the forces, secure control of the territory in" names a number of villages, continuing on to the next page in the English, and says, "the 15th Armoured Brigade deploy part of the forces to the general area of Pristina and put on standby for anti-landing combat in Kosovo plateau." And then it says: "Established control of the territory and law and order in the general area of Pristina." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So it would appear, sir, that on the 1st of April, 1999, that 15th Armoured Brigade was ordered to deploy to the general area of Pristina, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing for me to interpret here, that's the way it's written. I can say neither yes or no. They deployed as written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And their orders were to establish control of the territory and law and order in the general area of Pristina, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task they were given was the one that is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And they are an armoured brigade, sir, certainly they could well have used a tank or two or more if that was thought necessary, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I said that in Pristina there weren't any tanks, and I don't believe that the commander of the 15th Armoured Brigade at that time was Colonel Mladen Cirkovic could have used those tanks outside the zone that the corps commander ordered him to use them in. The corps commander did not order him to use them in Pristina. That can be seen from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, that's not what it appears to say to me, sir. It appears that they were, in fact, specifically ordered to establish control of the territory and law and order in the general area of Pristina. I believe you already answered that was correct.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the most problematic word here is the one that says "beyond." If it did not say "beyond," you would probably be right, but this way you are not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm following what you are saying, sir. Are you saying that they were not empowered and, in fact, ordered to establish law and order in Pristina generally?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say generally, in the general area of Pristina, beyond Pristina. Please, if the interpretation is not right, may it be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm asking if you can tell us what you understand it to mean.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand it -- well, now I'm going to tell you how I understand it. I understand it in this way: The commander should deploy his units in the general area, in the broader area. That is to say, at a distance from the city centre, from the town proper. In locations that lend themselves to his implementation of the tasks given to him by the commander. So that is the area that goes beyond the town itself. That is indeed the way it was. Now, where he exactly deployed them and what is the general area, the area beyond town, perhaps it's the commander or somebody from his staff who could explain that best to you. This is how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And that's fine, sir. I'm not sure that we're at odds. I'm not suggesting that the order required him to roll tanks down main street. I'm just saying that their order was to establish control and ensure that law and order was in place in the territory of Pristina, in that area. I don't think we're at odds, but let me show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we can see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, but we are at odds. Again you uttered the word Pristina, and you avoided using the word "beyond" as in broader area. That word should always accompany the word Pristina as is stated in this document. So in the broader or general area of Pristina. It's the adjective that's problematic here, or rather, it's not problematic, it means that it wasn't in Pristina itself. That means outside, beyond Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And yet their orders, sir, were to maintain law and order, presumably not by sitting outside in an isolated area. Sir, I don't want to go back and forth on this, I think we have your position.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your assumption is right on that.
