utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Filipovic, I would be interested in the following: During the war apart from Mr. Demaqi, who you mentioned, did you perhaps see in Pristina some other leaders of the Albania separatist movement?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. There were many. I've already mentioned Adem Demaqi. There was Veton Surroi and many others who were in favour of Kosovo becoming a republic. There were also people there who had had been sentenced to prison terms for terrorist acts and after leaving the prison they lived unhindered in Pristina or elsewhere. They could stroll about town without any problem. The Siptar members, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My learned friend asked you about the village of Gracanica and its function during the war. What about Ajvalija, where is it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ajvalija is along the road between Pristina and Gracanica. Approaching to Gracanica one needs to turn to the east from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the ethnic makeup of that village?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed two years of elementary education there, and during the aggression, in Ajvalija there were some 4.000 Siptars and between 2- and 300 Serb inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to Ajvalija during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. The population there mostly lived in harmony. There were no disputes or problems. There is a whole line of examples that can be used of the two ethnic groups helping each other. I remember the Jocic and Mitic families who were assisting the Siptars and vice-versa. They used to shop in the Vitija family shop, as well as the shops of the Drela and the Berisha families. The church operated throughout. That's was life was like in Ajvalija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to the village of Maticane during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the general area of Maticane and in Maticane itself. It is a large neighbourhood on the outskirts of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic makeup?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were only some 30 Serbs from the Vasic, Simic, and Kostic families. The other 4- to 5.000 inhabitants were Siptar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: During the war, as far as you know, did anyone move out of the village of Maticane?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Kostics, Simics, Vasics. There were many people with slit throats, many people kidnapped from Maticane. The Serbs moved out, whereas the known terrorists remained living in Maticane, and I can enumerate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this, rather: Do you know whether any Albanians were moved out of Maticane during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the Albanians did leave Maticane, but most of them remained. There were even two terrorists groups which clashed in Maticane. As a result of that, there were two killed. To date there is a cemetery containing their graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Kisnica during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few times. Especially when the corps command was deployed there in the broader area of Pristina. As far as I know there were Siptars mostly as well as several Serb families. The Kisnica mine operated properly and the employees were under work obligations so both Serb and Siptars came there to work. Many Siptars attended their work regularly. That would be it for the most part regarding Kisnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, Filipovic. I have no further questions for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, this concludes my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I have a question to the obstacles you mentioned the man-made and natural obstacles between Lapska Street and the cemetery. You just said obstacles, man-made and natural, can you describe them in more detail, please?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can describe them for you. Between Lapska Street and the Orthodox cemetery, I can tell you a few obstacles even though it's been quite a long time since I left the area. Let's start with the man-made buildings. There's the invest bank building in close proximity to the Municipal Assembly building. Next there is the Municipal Assembly building. Then the building in the former JNA street which is now called Kralja Milutina Street. There is the management building of the Kisnica mine close to number 46 where I attended military academy. There is another building close to Marko Isak Street which has five, six, or seven floors. There is a building close to the Omladina movie theatre. Then there are buildings close to the former Ljubljanska bank and the centre where William Walker was, which has eight or nine floors. Those are all obstacles en route to the Orthodox cemetery. Lapska Street and the Orthodox cemetery are approximately at the same attitude -- altitude. These obstacles alone prevent any visibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what about the natural obstacles in that direction?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the natural obstacles, there is a part close to the railroad which is higher than Lapska Street and this Orthodox cemetery. I don't know what the altitude is, but it is higher. Since the whole Pristina is at an altitude of some 570 metres above sea level, but it varies between 520 and 650 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now I would like to have a detailed explanation of the obstacles between the Lapska Street and Lukare, you said the same man-made and natural obstacles.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are both man-made and natural obstacle, but there are more of the natural ones. Those are tall trees and lie of the land. However, there are some man-made obstacles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I have another question, just a moment. This morning you spoke about -- I would like to take you back to a page 21, line 12. And I would like to quote: "I think it was Brnjica, although in the general area of Grmija there were parts of such missiles found. So the general area of Pristina, Gornja Brnjica," and so on. "The general area of Devet Jugovica and the other areas of Pristina. We collected such parts." Then you continue: "I even wanted to present you with a list of those parts." The last sentence I really didn't understand in this context. Could you explain that a little more detailed.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mostly had in mind different parts of missiles. There were cluster bomb parts, there were parts of projectiles with uranium charge, then there were parts of Tomahawks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, perhaps you didn't understand my question. You said, so it's written in the transcript: "I even wanted to present you with a list of those parts." Did you mean that you wanted orally to present such a list, or what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. I wanted to enumerate them orally, that's what I mean by list, and I've already done so partially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may be able to help me with one matter. If we could have Exhibit D722 on the screen, please. Do you remember that you were shown this map of the Pristina area and you marked three locations: Gracanica, Obilic, and Goles, I think. You then drew the circle number 4, and you said that outside of that circle was the broader area of Pristina. What made you decide that the broader area of Pristina was outside the circle you had drawn?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you mind repeating, the microphones were turned off.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I circled this, what I had in mind was the constructed part of Pristina, that is to say where the buildings are and the territory of the municipality of Pristina. The circle does not represent the territory of the municipality. It is far bigger. In diameter it's about 50 kilometres. And it goes from the north-east from Kobila and Kacikovski [phoen] then down south to the municipal border with the Lipljan municipality and Kosovo municipality and Obilic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Kosovo Polje municipality and Obilic.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I circled this believing that this was the general area of Pristina, however, the municipality of Pristina is a much bigger area outside the circle I drew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So this was really your own general description of what might be a broader area of Pristina, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should be it more or less, but no one ever determined the exact borders. It is usually believed that the general area is what is outside the constructed, the urban part of the town itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The area you have circled though is much more extensive than the actual built-up area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is quite bigger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We wish to thank you for your attendance here in The Hague again, for the assistance that you've been able to give, and you are now, of course, able to return to your normal activities. And a Court Officer will show you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you and greetings to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's probably a bit late, Mr. Djurdjic to call your next witness now? We want to draw attention once more to the slow progress. This is just, I believe, the 13th of your Defence witnesses that has been completed. It has taken us over four weeks, that's excluding, of course, the evidence of the accused. And what we notice is that in the original estimate where you thought you might take until the end of May, times were allowed for each of these witnesses. And you are now providing revised time estimates which are double or longer the time in the original estimate. That seems to have been the clear pattern to date. Thankfully, the Prosecution is generally being very brief in its cross-examination. If it was taking anything like the time you have been taking and your colleagues, with your examination-in-chief and re-examination our progress would be lamentably slow. It is the case that you have indicated that five witnesses on your original list will not be called, but even so, we are well behind the original timetable. Now, this can't just be allowed to carry on or we will be hearing witnesses in June and July, and that's not going to be in anybody's interests. It is our observation that you appear to be dealing with many matters that are not central to this case, and that the examination-in-chief could be much shorter. If you concentrated on what are the allegations in the indictment and concentrated your evidence on those, that is especially so in the case of witnesses that are Rule 92 ter witnesses where there has been a clear tendency to have the witness go over lots of the evidence that has been tendered by way of statement or transcript, to have a repeat canvassing of that evidence. This has been raised with yourself and Mr. Djordjevic and I think Mr. Popovic on more than one occasion so far, but there seems to be no significant change in the rate of progress. Is there any encouragement you can give us at this point, Mr. Djurdjic, about the time taken with witnesses and the rate of progress? We would indicate that if there isn't really some significant change, the Chamber will have to consider imposing arbitrary time-limits on you and that, of course, is something we've tried to avoid doing to give you the greatest opportunity to present your case in the best way. I'll stop speaking and see if you are in a position to offer us something at this point, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must underline once more that this Defence is particularly pleased with the way this Chamber has proceeded in this case and that you have not adhered to some procedures we were witness to in other cases. I am sorry for our inability to assess correctly the time we would need for certain witnesses given that we lacked any previous experience in that regard. And we wanted to shed some light on certain aspects which have not been in the focus of previous Defence teams. Despite all that, I assure you that our Defence case will last significantly shorter than what you said, and that the time that we will use in excess will be compensated for by not calling certain witnesses, and I don't believe I said initially it was supposed to be the end of May, but until the end of April. However, it is my objective assessment at this moment that our case should rest by mid-April because if we have a witness here covering a certain aspect or area, we will remove from the list all other witnesses that were supposed to address the same issue. We distributed our witnesses into several categories and we are now closing the first category. Although, initially, I believe there would be more in that category. What is left now is the police and the political category of witnesses, if I may say so, and some expert witnesses in the end. I can assure you that we will not waste time unduly. I believe my assessment about the close of our case is quite realistic in these terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Djurdjic. There are a couple of comments I would make at the moment. You have earlier indicated, you and Mr. Djordjevic, that it is anticipated that some witnesses on the list would not be called beyond the five that have already been specified. It's going to save a great deal of effort by the Chamber and by the Prosecution if we are given some indication of the witnesses you will not be calling. Now, I appreciate that you may not be able to do that for every witness because a lot will depend upon how a particular witness goes or whether there is difficulty with one witness and you have to call a substitute and so on, but there will no doubt be a number of witnesses which you can identify now and that will save us a deal of preparation time, and also the Prosecution if they can be identified now and if as soon as others become clear we are progressively told of those. If you could give that thought over the weekend, we may be able to shorten your list somewhat. And that will help us see a little more clearly what lies ahead. The second comment I want to make is that we are conscious that you will have been fairly pressed with witnesses, and we were thinking of having a shorter break over Easter, a short break over Easter, so that you could expect not to have to call witnesses immediately after Easter or the week following that. That could mean that your programme may extend toward the end of April to finish rather than be finished by mid-April, but one of the objects of that will be enable Mr. Djordjevic and yourself to review your evidence and be sure that, A, you haven't overlooked some witness or matter, and that, B, you really do need to call any witnesses that remain on your list. So if you would keep that in mind as well. In due course we'll fix the clear dates when we won't sit so that you can make the plans for the travel of your witnesses that are necessary. But if you and the Prosecution will keep in mind that we will have a short break over the Easter period, which we hope will be of benefit to yourself in the finalisation of the shape of your Defence case. So if we could ask you then over the weekend to look at your witness list and you may be able to be a little more clear and positive early next week about the shape of your future list. We will adjourn now until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
